TENTATIVE RULING FOR February 10, 2026
Department S22 – Judge David Driscoll
This court follows California Rules of Court, rule 3.1308(b) for tentative rulings. (See San
Bernardino Superior Court Local Emergency Rule 8.) Tentative rulings for each law & motion
will be posted on the internet (https://www.sb-court.org) by 3:00 p.m. on the court day
immediately before the hearing.
You may appear in person at the hearing although remote appearance by CourtCall is preferred
during the Pandemic. (See www.sb-court.org/general-information/remote-access ).
If you do not have Internet access or if you experience difficulty with the posted tentative ruling,
you may obtain the tentative ruling by calling the department (S-22) at (909) 521-3529 or the
Administrative Assistant (909) 708-8756, who prepared the ruling.
If you (or both parties) wish to submit on the Tentative, notify the other party and call the
department by 4:00 pm the day before and your appearance may be excused unless the
Court orders you to appear.
You must appear at the hearing if you are so directed by the court in the tentative ruling. Be
prepared to address those issues set forth by the court in its ruling.
UNLESS OTHERWISE NOTED, THE PREVAILING PARTY IS TO GIVE NOTICE OF THE
RULING.
____________________________________________________________________________
CIVSB2227886
CHERYLL PARKER v. VICTOR VALLEY UNION HIGH SCHOOL DISTRICT
____________________________________________________________________________
TENTATIVE RULING
This is a childhood sexual assault case. On December 15, 2022, Plaintiff Cheryll Parker filed a Complaint
against DOES 1 through 25.
On March 16, 2023, Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint, as of right, which added Defendant Victor
Valley Union High School District (“District”), and alleges the following causes of action:
(1) Negligence, against the District;
(2) Negligence, against DOES 2 through 25;
(3) Negligent Hiring, Retention and Supervision, against the District;
(4) Negligent Hiring, Retention and Supervision, against DOES 2 through 25
Plaintiff alleges that in approximately 1986, when Plaintiff was approximately 15 years old and was a
student at the District, Plaintiff was sexually abused and assaulted by Elvin Lee Momon, Plaintiff’s
school counselor, approximately 4 to 5 times over a period of approximately one year while at school and
at Plaintiff’s home. During the ongoing course of the aforementioned sexual abuse, there were numerous
rumors over many years regarding Momon having sexual relationships with students. Additionally,
Momon would spend long periods of time alone with Plaintiff in Momon’s office. Despite the foregoing,
no action was taken, no investigation was completed, and Momon continued to sexually abuse and assault
Plaintiff. (FAC ¶¶ 29-33.)
Now before the Court is the District’s Motion Compelling Further Responses to Production of Documents
(Set Two), filed on October 30, 2025.
Analysis
The District seeks an order compelling further responses to RFP No. 12, which requires the Plaintiff to
produce “[t]he statement taken of Elvin Momon on or about December 6, 2022, whether written or
recorded form.” In response, Plaintiff objected to this request on the basis that Plaintiff asserts the
statements are protected by the attorney work product doctrine and/or “investigator privilege.” Under
California law, privileges are strictly governed by statute. (HLC Properties, Ltd. v. Superior Court (2005)
35 Cal.4th 54, 59.) Courts may not add to the statutory privileges except as required by state or federal
constitutional law. (Roberts v. City of Palmdale (1993) 5 Cal.4th 363, 373.) Here, there does not appear to
be any “investigator privilege” and Plaintiff does not argue the existence of such in opposition. As such,
only Plaintiff’s attorney work-product doctrine privilege will be analyzed.
Notably, while RFP No. 12 requests the Plaintiff to produce “statements” made by Momon during an
informal interview conducted by an investigator hired by Plaintiff’s Counsel, approximately nine days
before the Action was filed, it appears that the District is, in actuality, seeking the production of the
investigator’s report or notes as the District does not dispute Plaintiff’s Counsel’s representations that the
interview was never recorded and that Momon neither provided a written statement nor signed a written
statement. (Jones Decl. ¶ 4.) Plaintiff’s opposing papers state that it was a telephonic interview conducted
by an employee of plaintiff’s counsel’s law firm with notes of the conversation prepared by an
investigator employed and trained by the law firm.
Code of Civil Procedure section 2018.010, et seq., codifies the attorney “work product” doctrine and
specifies the conditions under which disclosure of an attorney’s “work product” may be compelled.
(McKesson HBOC, Inc. v. Superior Court (2004) 115 Cal.App.4th 1229, 1238.) Its stated purpose is to
preserve the rights of attorneys in the preparation of their cases and to prevent attorneys from taking
advantage of the industry and creativity of opposing counsel. (State Comp. Ins. Fund v. Superior Court
(2001) 91 Cal.App.4th 1080, 1091.) The attorney is the exclusive holder of the privilege and is the only
person who has standing to assert the privilege. (Ibid.)
The attorney work-product doctrine is divided into two categories, absolute and qualified work product.
Any writing that reflects an attorney’s impressions, conclusions, opinions or legal research or theories is
not discoverable at any time. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2018.030, subd. (a).) However, any work product other
than those writings described in subsection (a) are not discoverable, unless the court determines that
denial of the discovery will unfairly prejudice the party seeking discovery in preparing the party’s claim
or defense or will result in an injustice. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2018.030, subd. (b); Coito v. Superior Court
(2012) 54 Cal.4th 480, 488 (Coito).)
In Coito, the California Supreme Court held that a witness statement obtained through an attorney-
directed interview is entitled as a matter of law to at least qualified work product protection. (Coito,
supra, 54 Cal.4th at pp. 496-497, 499.) However, writings that contain an attorney’s mental impressions,
opinions, conclusions and theories are absolutely protected—i.e., no compelled disclosure under any
circumstances. (Id. at pp. 486, 494-497, 499-500.)
The District argues that Plaintiff’s Counsel waived the protections of the attorney “work product”
doctrine when he deposed Momon on June 26, 2025, specifically by asking Momon about the statements
he gave to the investigator on December 6, 2022, while in the presence of the District’s Counsel, the
District’s Director of Risk Management, and Momon’s attorney who also attended the deposition.
In general, no statutory provision governs waiver of work product protection. (Raytheon Co. v. Superior
Court (1989) 208 Cal.App.3d 683, 688.) But California courts have recognized that the waiver doctrine is
applicable to the work product rule as well as to the attorney-client privilege. (Wells Fargo Bank v.
Superior Court (2000) 22 Cal.4th 201, 214.) The work product protection may be waived “by the
attorney’s disclosure or consent to disclosure to a person, other than the client, who has no interest in
maintaining the confidentiality ... of a significant part of the work product.” (OXY Resources California
LLC v. Superior Court (2004) 115 Cal.App.4th 874, 891.) Thus, work product protection “is not waived
except by a disclosure wholly inconsistent with the purpose of the privilege, which is to safeguard the
attorney’s work product and trial preparation. (Ibid.) An implied waiver may also be found when a party
“has put the otherwise privileged communication directly at issue and ... disclosure is essential for a fair
adjudication of the action.” (People v. Superior Court (Jones) (2021) 12 Cal.5th 348, 363.)
Here, during Momon’s deposition, the following questions were posed by Plaintiff’s Counsel:
• Whether Momon could recall discussing the case from someone from Plaintiff’s Counsel’s
Office? (Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 26:14-21.)
• Whether Momon could provide a rough ballpark estimate as to when the interview occurred?
(Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 26:25-27:3.)
• A general question asking what Momon could recall during the interview. (Reeves Decl. Exh. C at
26:25-27:3.)
• Whether Momon could recall if the investigator asked him if he ever conducted personal sessions
with any of Momon’s students? (Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 28:2-5.)
• Whether Momon knew where Plaintiff lived, how Momon knew that particular fact, and whether
Momon had previously given Plaintiff a ride home from school. (Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 28:6-23.)
• How Momon came to know Plaintiff, and whether Plaintiff was assigned to Momon in his role as
a school counselor? (Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 28:24-30:2.)
• Whether Momon had provided Plaintiff or other student with a drive home on any other occasion?
(Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 32:4-12.)
• Whether Momon could recall the investigator asking Momon whether he had given personal
sessions with students at their home? (Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 32:13-33:12.)
• Whether Momon had any type of romantic relationship or sexual intercourse with Plaintiff or any
students while working for the District? (Reeves Decl. Exh. C at 35:2-16.)
Upon considering this evidence, although Plaintiff’s Counsel revealed the existence of the interview and
also disclosed the substance of several prior questions asked during the interview, Plaintiff’s Counsel did
not cross-examine Momon with any possible inconsistencies made during the interview and did not reveal
any information related to Plaintiff’s Counsel’s impressions, conclusions, opinions or legal research or
theories. At most, it appears that Plaintiff’s Counsel waived the substance of the questions and
statements made by Momon during the interview, but did not waive any internal impressions,
conclusions, opinions, etc. However, to the extent that the investigator’s notes may contain such
confidential matters, an in-camera inspection of the report would therefore be warranted (Evidence Code
§915(b)), which would allow the Court to better determine if the absolute or qualified privilege applies,
and whether, in the latter event, disclosure should be compelled. (See Coito, supra, 54 Cal.4th at p. 496
[outlining the potential need for an in-camera review].)
TENTATIVE RULING
The court will take this matter under submission and suspend its final ruling on RPD No. 12 until it has
completed an in-camera review of the investigative report. If it is determined that the investigative report
contains Plaintiff’s Counsel’s confidential impressions, conclusions, opinions or legal research or
theories, the court will order those matters be redacted. The court will order production of the remainder
of the report based upon its finding of a waiver as a result of plaintiff counsel’s deposition questioning
regarding the substance of questions posed during the witness’ interview.
